## Introduction

If you build AI products, sooner or later you end up stitching together a
small orchestra of tools:

- local scripts
- API calls
- logs
- config files
- containers
- CI pipelines

The shell is often the quickest way to make these components cooperate.
This tutorial starts at the very beginning and works up to practical
"glue work" you can apply in real AI engineering tasks.

### Intended Audience

Engineers who are comfortable writing code but have little (or no) shell
experience. If you're already fluent in shell, skip ahead to process control
and service debugging.

### What You'll Need

- [ ] A terminal (local shell, or the browser sandbox in this article)
- [ ] Basic familiarity with files and folders
- [ ] Curiosity and willingness to try small experiments

## How To Use This Article

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Sandbox Rules (Please Read)

- The interactive shell runs in a simulated bash sandbox in your browser, not your local machine.
- Sessions are ephemeral. Refreshing the page usually resets your environment.
- Do **not** paste secrets, tokens, private keys, or credentials.
- This is not full Linux parity (process/network commands may differ from your laptop).
- Commands here are intentionally low-risk and learning-oriented.
:::

Open the **shell sandbox** panel at the bottom of the page when you want to
practice. It loads once and stays available as you scroll through the tutorial.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
### Why not a full Linux VM?

An embedded full Linux VM (like linuxontab) boots Alpine, runs `apk update`, and
installs packages before you get a prompt — often 30–60+ seconds. This sandbox
uses **just-bash**, a simulated shell that starts in a few seconds. It is ideal
for learning `grep`, pipes, permissions, and file operations. For full-fidelity
process and port debugging, use your local terminal or Codespaces (see section 8).
:::

## Hints and Tips

A handful of habits that pay off immediately. These are worth learning early,
before the command vocabulary gets more involved.

### Use arrow keys to navigate prior commands (work smart, not hard)

The shell remembers commands you have already run. You do not need to retype a
long pipeline every time you want to tweak it.

- **Up arrow** — step back through previous commands
- **Down arrow** — step forward again through that history

This is especially useful when you are iterating on something fiddly: a `grep`
chain, a `curl` call with flags, or a script you keep running with small edits.
Run the command once, press **Up**, adjust a word or two, press **Enter**.

### Try It

Open the sandbox and run a few different commands, then use the arrow keys to
bring an earlier one back to the prompt without retyping it.

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

### Use Tab to complete matches

Tab completion is the shell's way of finishing your typing for you. Start a
command or path, press **Tab**, and the shell suggests the rest based on what
exists in your current directory or what it recognises as a valid command name.

- Type the first few letters of a filename, then press **Tab**
- If there is only one match, the shell fills in the rest
- If there are several matches, press **Tab** again (or twice quickly) to see
  the options

This saves time and cuts down on typos — particularly handy for long paths like
`project/src/eval_metrics.py` when you only need to type `project/src/e` and
hit **Tab**.

### Try It

In the sandbox, create a file with `touch my-long-filename.txt`, then type
`cat my-l` and press **Tab** to complete the name before pressing **Enter**.

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

### Jump around the command line with modifier keys

Once a command gets long, tapping the arrow key character-by-character is
painful. On macOS, modifier keys let you move in bigger jumps:

- **⌘ + ←** — jump to the start of the line
- **⌘ + →** — jump to the end of the line
- **⌥ + ←** — jump back one word at a time
- **⌥ + →** — jump forward one word at a time

This is useful when you need to fix a typo in the middle of a pipeline without
retyping the whole thing. Jump to the word, edit it, **Enter**.

On Linux terminals, the equivalents are usually **Ctrl+A** / **Ctrl+E** for the
start and end of the line, and **Alt + ←** / **Alt + →** to move word by word.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The browser sandbox may not support every macOS shortcut. If a key combo does
nothing, try the same exercise in your local terminal or Codespaces.
:::

### Try It

Type a long command such as `grep ERROR app.log | grep -v retry | wc -l`, then
use **⌘ + ←** and **⌥ + →** to move the cursor without retyping. On Linux, try
**Ctrl+A** and **Alt + →** instead.

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

## 1) Shell Fundamentals

We'll begin with a tiny command set that you will use repeatedly.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
pwd          # print current directory
ls           # list files/folders
ls -la       # include hidden files and details
cd /tmp      # change directory
cd -         # jump back to previous directory
```

### Try It

Run the commands above in the sandbox and answer:

1. Which directory are you in?
2. Which entries are hidden (start with `.`)?
3. What changed after `cd -`?

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

## 2) Data Flow: Pipes and Redirection

The shell gets powerful when you connect simple tools together.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
printf "apple\nbanana\napricot\n" > fruits.txt
cat fruits.txt
grep '^a' fruits.txt
grep '^a' fruits.txt | wc -l
```

- `>` writes output to a file (overwrites existing content).
- `|` passes output from one command into the next.

### Try It

Add one more fruit, then count how many begin with `b`.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
echo "blueberry" >> fruits.txt
grep '^b' fruits.txt | wc -l
```

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

## 3) Grep Chaining

`grep` is one of the best shell tools for quick investigations.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
printf "INFO startup\nWARN cache_miss\nERROR timeout\nERROR retry_failed\n" > app.log
cat app.log | grep 'ERROR' | grep -v 'retry'
```

This approach is useful for narrowing noisy logs quickly:

1. broad match (`ERROR`)
2. exclude known noise (`-v retry`)

### AI Engineer Use Case

When a local model service fails, this pattern helps isolate relevant errors
before you disappear into a debugging rabbit hole.

## 4) Brace Expansion and Globs

Brace expansion is a tiny feature that saves surprising amounts of time.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
mkdir -p project/{data,src,tests,logs}
touch project/src/{ingest,embed,serve}.py
ls -R project
```

This is great for scaffolding small prototypes quickly.

### Try It

Create a second set of files for evaluation scripts in one command.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
touch project/src/{eval_metrics,eval_runner}.py
```

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

## 5) Executables and Permissions

A script file is not executable by default, even if it contains valid shell
code.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
cat > hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Hello from shell"
EOF

ls -l hello.sh
./hello.sh
```

You should see a permission error before adding execute permission. That's
normal.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
chmod +x hello.sh
ls -l hello.sh
./hello.sh
```

This pattern matters when packaging helper scripts for teammates, automation,
or CI jobs.

## 6) Processes, Ports, and Signals

Now we're in classic operations/debugging territory.

### Start and inspect a process

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
sleep 300 &
jobs
ps -ef | grep sleep | grep -v grep
```

### Stop a process gracefully

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
kill <PID>
```

### Force stop (last resort)

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
kill -9 <PID>
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Use `kill -9` sparingly. It bypasses graceful shutdown and can leave temporary
state or partial writes behind.
:::

### Check which process is using a port

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
lsof -i :8000
```

In real projects, this is often the fastest answer to:
"Why won't my service start on this port?"

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Browser sandboxes may not perfectly reproduce host networking behavior. For
full-fidelity `lsof -i`, signals, and service debugging, run these commands in
your local terminal or GitHub Codespaces.
:::

## 7) Practical AI Glue Workflows

These small shell pipelines can save a lot of time during development.

### Filter noisy logs

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
cat app.log | grep 'ERROR' | grep -v 'healthcheck'
```

### Quick file inventory

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
ls -R project | grep '\.py$'
```

### Verify executable helpers

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
ls -l *.sh
```

## 8) Extension: Run Advanced Commands Locally or in Codespaces

If you want full-fidelity behavior for advanced tasks:

1. Run locally on your machine, or
2. Open the repository in GitHub and press `.` for browser VSCode
3. Launch Codespaces for an interactive terminal

This is the best environment for realistic process and network debugging.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Why bother with the local run?

The browser sandbox is excellent for learning command syntax and flow. Your
local machine or Codespaces is where process IDs, ports, services, and real
filesystem state behave as expected for production debugging.
:::

## 9) Pre-Publish Checklist For Your Own Shell Docs

- Are all interactive commands safe and reversible?
- Did you clearly warn readers not to paste secrets?
- Did you distinguish sandbox behavior from real host behavior?
- Are advanced commands (`kill -9`, `lsof -i`) explained with caution?
- Does each section include a concrete "why this matters" use case?

## Wrap-up

Shell skills compound quickly. Start with navigation and pipes, add pattern
matching, permissions, and process control, then apply them to your own tool
chain. Once these habits click, the shell becomes a dependable orchestration
layer for AI engineering work.
